tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 1. Games as Systems. In December 2023, a 13-year-old from Oklahoma named Willis Gibson did something no human player was known to have done in the 34 years since Nintendo released its home console version of Tetris: he played until the game itself broke. Partway through level 157, the screen froze. The programmers had never expected anyone to get that far. For decades, top players had treated level 29, where pieces fall almost too fast to steer, as the practical end. Then players invented ways of beating it, including “rolling,” a technique of drumming the back of the controller against a resting thumb to move pieces faster. Not one rule of the game had changed since 1989. The behavior that broke it was hiding in a short list of rules all along, waiting for players to find it. That gap between a few rules and what they produce is the subject of this chapter. This first chapter gives you the three ideas the rest of the book is built on. Section 1.1 asks what a game is, comparing the definitions that philosophers and designers actually use. Section 1.2 introduces the MDA framework, which traces how rules (mechanics) produce patterns of play (dynamics) and, through them, player experience (aesthetics). Section 1.3 gives you a parts list, Tracy Fullerton’s formal and dramatic elements, for taking any game apart. You will meet the book’s running examples, Tetris, Super Mario Bros. and Slay the Spire, and at the end you will write the first rules for your own pocket card game, which you will improve in every chapter that follows.

tracks.label: 1.1 Defining a game
tracks.text: Section 1 point 1. Defining a game. People have argued about what counts as a game for a long time. In Philosophical Investigations (1953), Ludwig Wittgenstein used games as his main example of a word whose members share no single feature, only overlapping resemblances, like the faces in a family. The philosopher Bernard Suits, who taught at the University of Waterloo in Canada, took that as a challenge. In The Grasshopper: Games, Life and Utopia (1978), a book written as dialogues between Aesop’s grasshopper and his followers, he set out to show that games do share a definition after all. Designers care about this argument for a practical reason. A good definition lists the parts a game cannot do without, and every part on that list is something you can design, tune or break. Suits’s short version is famous: “playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles”. His full version has four parts. There is a prelusory goal, a state of affairs you can describe before any game exists, such as a ball resting in a hole. There are constitutive rules, which forbid the most efficient ways of reaching that goal. There are lusory means, the ways of acting that the rules still allow. And there is the lusory attitude, the player’s acceptance of the rules just because they make the activity possible. Golf is his clearest case. The easiest way to get a ball into a hole is to walk over and drop it in. Golfers instead stand far away and hit it with a club, and they do it on purpose. Game designers have offered definitions built for their own work. Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, in Rules of Play (2003), define a game as “a system in which players engage in an artificial conflict, defined by rules, that results in a quantifiable outcome”. System is the word this book leans on hardest: a game is a set of parts whose relationships produce behavior. Artificial marks the conflict as set apart from ordinary life, an idea Salen and Zimmerman connect to the historian Johan Huizinga’s image of the magic circle, the special space and time inside which a game’s rules hold. Jesper Juul, in Half-Real (2005), surveyed earlier definitions and proposed a classic game model with six features: rules, a variable and quantifiable outcome, values attached to the possible outcomes, player effort, a player who cares about the outcome, and real-life consequences that are negotiable. Definitions earn their keep at the edges. Juul places open-ended simulations, in which no outcome counts as winning, among his borderline cases rather than inside or outside the category. Jane McGonigal, in Reality Is Broken (2011), drew on Suits to boil the tradition down to four traits she argues all games share: a goal, rules, a feedback system and voluntary participation. Her list is the one this section uses, because each trait points at a designer’s job. The goal aims the player’s attention. The rules make reaching it interesting. The feedback system tells players how close they are. Voluntary participation means the player accepts all three, and can walk away at any time. Run Tetris (1984) through those four traits. Its goal is unusual: in its classic endless mode you cannot win, so the real goal is to clear rows and score as much as possible before the stack reaches the top. Its rules are few. In the familiar versions, seven shapes fall into a well ten cells wide and twenty tall, full rows vanish, and the pieces speed up as you clear more rows. Its feedback is constant, from the flash of a cleared row to the score, the level number and the height of the stack itself, which you read at a glance (Figure 1.1). And nobody has to play it. Because players can quit at any moment, a game has to keep earning their attention, which is why feedback, pacing and difficulty each get a chapter later in this book. A common misconception: If nobody wins or loses, it isn’t really a game. In fact, None of the definitions in this section require a winner. Salen and Zimmerman ask for a quantifiable outcome and Juul for outcomes with different values, and a score meets both. Endless Tetris and many single-player games have no victory at all, only better and worse results.

tracks.label: 1.2 The MDA framework
tracks.text: Section 1 point 2. The MDA framework. In 2004, Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek published a short paper, “MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research,” at a workshop of the American Association for Artificial Intelligence. The framework was not new to them. They had developed it and taught it at the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference in San Jose from 2001 to 2004. MDA splits a game into three layers. Mechanics “describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.” Dynamics are the run-time behavior that appears when the mechanics act on player inputs and on each other over time. Aesthetics are the emotional responses the game aims to evoke in the player as they interact with it. The framework’s most useful idea is that designers and players meet the same game from opposite ends (Figure 1.2). A designer works from mechanics outward: you write rules, watch the dynamics they produce, and hope those dynamics create the aesthetics you were aiming for. A player starts at the other end. They feel the tension or the delight first, notice patterns of play second, and may never think about the underlying rules at all. Salen and Zimmerman call game design a second-order design problem for the same reason: designers shape play only indirectly, by setting up the rules from which play emerges. You cannot write “the player feels clever” into a rulebook. You can only write rules and then test whether they make players feel clever. MDA also replaced the vague word fun with a vocabulary. The paper lists eight kinds of aesthetic, each with a short gloss: Sensation (game as sense-pleasure), Fantasy (game as make-believe), Narrative (game as drama), Challenge (game as obstacle course), Fellowship (game as social framework), Discovery (game as uncharted territory), Expression (game as self-discovery) and Submission (game as pastime). The authors say plainly that the list is not complete and that most games pursue several aesthetics at once; their profile of the Final Fantasy series (from 1987) combines Fantasy, Narrative, Expression, Discovery, Challenge and Submission. Naming the target has practical effects. A team that agrees it is making a Challenge game will cut and keep different features from a team making a Fellowship game, even with the same theme. Watch the three layers work in Tetris. In the 1989 version for the Nintendo Entertainment System, one mechanic is the scoring table. Clearing one row scores 40 points times the level plus one, while clearing four rows at once, a move players call a tetris, scores 1,200 times the level plus one. Four single clears are worth 160 points at level 0; one tetris is worth 7.5 times as much. That single mechanic produces a dynamic every skilled player knows. They stack pieces high, keep one column empty, and wait for the long straight piece. The stack climbs while they wait, and the aesthetic that results is Challenge, laced with tension and relief. The rules never tell anyone to build a well and gamble. They just make it the best strategy, and players found it. Dynamics include what players do with their hands and eyes. In a 1994 study, the cognitive scientists David Kirsh and Paul Maglio found that Tetris players often rotate a falling piece more than its final placement requires. The extra turns are not errors. Turning the piece on screen can be quicker than turning it in your head, so players use the game itself as a thinking aid. Kirsh and Maglio called such moves epistemic actions: actions taken to gain information or make thinking easier, rather than to move closer to the goal. MDA has limits worth knowing. It says little about fiction and theme, which Juul argues matter alongside rules in video games, and its use of aesthetics for emotions confuses people who expect the word to mean art style. As a way to trace rules to experience, it is still the standard starting point, and you will use it in every chapter. A common misconception: In MDA, “aesthetics” means the graphics and art style. In fact, In MDA, aesthetics are the player’s emotional responses, such as Challenge or Fellowship. Art and sound help produce them, especially Sensation, but a game made of plain colored blocks, like Tetris, can be rich in aesthetics.

tracks.label: 1.3 Formal and dramatic elements
tracks.text: Section 1 point 3. Formal and dramatic elements. MDA tells you how rules turn into experience, but it does not give you a parts list. For that, many designers use the vocabulary of Tracy Fullerton, who teaches game design at the University of Southern California, set out in Game Design Workshop, now in its fifth edition (2024). Fullerton defines a game as “a closed, formal system that engages players in structured conflict and resolves its uncertainty in an unequal outcome”. She divides a game’s structure into eight formal elements: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries and outcome. Her test of the list is to take a familiar card game such as gin rummy and change or remove one element at a time. Remove the objective and play loses its point; change a procedure and the game takes on a different character. Take Super Mario Bros. (1985) as a first case. Players: one, or two taking turns. Objectives: reach the end of each level, usually marked by a flagpole, and, finally, rescue Princess Toadstool (called Peach in Japan, a name later used everywhere) from Bowser. Procedures are the actions players take and the methods of play: press A to jump, hold B to run. Rules define the game’s objects and what is allowed: stomping a Goomba defeats it, touching one from the side costs Mario his power-up or a life, and a Super Mushroom makes him big. Fullerton separates procedures from rules because they answer different questions. Procedures say what the player does; rules say what those actions mean and what the game forbids. In a paper game the difference is visible on the page, while in a video game the code enforces both. Slay the Spire, a deck-building game from the small studio Mega Crit, shows the other four (Figure 1.3). Its resources are many: hit points that carry from fight to fight, three energy per turn to spend on cards, gold for shops, the cards themselves, relics with passive powers, and potions. Conflict comes from enemies, and one of the game’s cleverest rules is that each enemy shows its intent for the coming turn, such as an attack of a stated size, so the player’s problem becomes planning rather than guessing. Its boundaries are a single run across a branching map. Its outcome is unequal in exactly Fullerton’s sense: you defeat the final boss or you die, and a new run begins from scratch. Its Ascension levels, which add handicaps for players who have already won, such as tougher enemies and scarcer resources, raise the difficulty of reaching that outcome while leaving the objective unchanged. Formal elements describe structure. Dramatic elements make players care about it. Fullerton’s core list is challenge, play, premise, character and story. Many students are surprised that the first two have nothing to do with plot. Tetris has no characters and no story, and its premise is barely more than falling blocks, yet it grips players through rising challenge and the endless small experiments of play. Super Mario Bros. adds a light premise, a plumber rescuing a princess, and that thin fiction does real work. Juul argues that a game’s fiction helps players understand its rules. A mushroom that makes Mario grow tells you, without a word of text, that mushrooms are good to collect. Together, the two lists form a diagnostic checklist. When a prototype feels flat, the cause is often an element nobody specified. A card game with no clear objective drifts. One with no conflict is a puzzle with nothing pushing back. One with no resource that players can run short of seldom forces hard choices. Boundaries need special care in physical games, because they include the shared agreement about when the game is on and off, the magic circle from section 1.1. You will use this checklist at the end of the chapter to write the first version of your pocket card game. Chapter 2 then looks at what players actually do moment to moment, and Chapter 4 returns to resources as a full economy. A common misconception: Dramatic elements just means the story, so abstract games like Tetris don’t have any. In fact, Story is only one of Fullerton’s five dramatic elements. Challenge and play are dramatic elements too, and they carry abstract games such as Tetris, which hold players without characters or plot.
